content: Despite the proven effectiveness of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) in alleviating asthma symptoms and reducing exacerbations, many patients fail to adhere fully to their prescribed ICS regimen. This suboptimal adherence is associated with worse clinical outcomes, increased healthcare utilization, and has been implicated in approximately one-third of asthma-related deaths in the UK. The reasons for non-adherence are multifaceted, and various interventions have been proposed to address this issue. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of interventions designed to improve adherence to ICS among individuals with asthma. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared interventions aimed at improving ICS adherence with usual care or alternative interventions. Eligible studies included both adults and children with asthma who had an active prescription for ICS, either as monotherapy or in combination with a long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA). The review identified 39 parallel RCTs, 28 of which contributed data to at least one meta-analysis. These trials involved a total of 16,303 participants, with follow-up durations ranging from two months to two years (median six months). Most studies were conducted in high-income countries. The trials were categorized into four main intervention types: adherence education, electronic trackers or reminders, simplified drug regimens, and school-based directly observed therapy. Two additional studies were described separately. Adherence education interventions demonstrated a 20-percentage-point improvement in adherence compared to control groups (95% confidence interval [CI]: 7.52 to 32.74; five studies; low-quality evidence). Electronic trackers or reminders improved adherence by 19 percentage points (95% CI: 14.47 to 25.26; six studies; moderate-quality evidence). Simplified drug regimens showed a smaller improvement of 4 percentage points (95% CI: 1.88 to 6.16; three studies; moderate-quality evidence). However, the quality of evidence was downgraded due to risks of bias and inconsistency across studies. Despite these improvements in adherence, the interventions did not consistently translate into significant clinical benefits. Pooled analyses did not show clear advantages for primary clinical outcomes, such as reductions in exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids (OCS) or improvements in asthma control. Similarly, secondary outcomes, including unscheduled healthcare visits and quality of life, showed no consistent benefits. The evidence for these outcomes ranged from very low to moderate quality. Some individual studies reported benefits, such as fewer unscheduled visits or reduced OCS use, but these findings were not consistent across the included trials. Data on school or work absences were often skewed and difficult to interpret, and adverse events were rarely measured or reported. Studies investigating school-based ICS administration did not assess adherence, exacerbations requiring OCS, asthma control, or adverse events. One study reported fewer unscheduled visits, while another found no differences; these data could not be pooled for analysis. In conclusion, while various interventions can improve adherence to ICS, the clinical significance of these improvements remains uncertain due to inconsistent and unclear impacts on clinical outcomes such as asthma control and quality of life. The confidence in these findings is limited by concerns about bias and inconsistency. Future research should focus on defining evidence-based thresholds for acceptable adherence, utilizing objective adherence measures, and employing validated tools and questionnaires. Additionally, covert monitoring and blinding or active control measures may help isolate the effects of the intervention from the influence of trial participation itself.
